moltenvk.note: MoltenVK 1.4.1 rebuilt with two Highball patches (spike/patches/moltenvk-shadow-import.patch and moltenvk-linear-fallback.patch, Scripts/build-moltenvk.sh). Shadow import is off unless a launch sets MVK_SHADOW_IMPORT=1 (32-bit native-Vulkan games such as The Sims Legacy Collection). Linear fallback is always on: a linear-tiled image that Metal cannot back with linear memory (3D, mipmapped or array images) is created with optimal tiling instead of failing vkCreateImage, which is what takes Red Dead Redemption 2 from an exit at 98 per cent to the main menu and the story.

notes: r6 (2026-09-11): r5 plus the MoltenVK linear-fallback patch. Red Dead Redemption 2 loads, reaches its main menu and starts the story on this engine (M1 Pro, macOS 26.6.2, 1280x720 windowed, about 60 fps in menus); every earlier engine exits at 98 per cent of the first load because MoltenVK refuses the game's linear 3D, mipmapped and array images. Nothing else changed from r5.

r5 (2026-09-09): r4 plus patch 0008, the fiber mirror. Marvel's Guardians of the Galaxy reaches gameplay on this engine and crashes on Play Game on every earlier one, verified twice from a clean start on an M1 Pro, macOS 26.6.2, at 27.5 fps in the opening scene. A reproducer that needs no game (private/notes/fibertest4.c) faults identically to the game on r4 and runs clean here.

Cost of 0008, measured: offset 0x20 holds the thread's pthread QoS class on macOS, so a thread that uses fibers loses that scheduling hint. Windows and macOS both fix that offset, so a correct GetCurrentFiber() and an intact QoS cache cannot coexist. Confined to threads that call the fiber APIs, and a stress run of 8 threads and 6.4M switches showed TLS and thread creation unaffected (320000 wrong fiber values on r4, 0 here).

Optional engine (2026-09-07): Highball's own build of the CrossOver 26.3 Wine tree (Wine 11.0) with the same DXMT, D3DMetal, MoltenVK and Template runtime as the default engine. Not the default: a bottle moves to it from its Advanced settings, or Highball offers it when a launcher's recipe names it (the EA app). Verified here: EA app install and sign-in, The Sims 4 through it (DXMT, 128 fps on an M1 Pro), Steam with GTA V install, Rockstar launcher sign-in window, Ubisoft Connect window.

Games were not re-verified on this engine (CS:GO's cascaded shadow maps are known to differ), which is why it is offered for the launchers that need it, one environment at a time, and never becomes the default on its own. Steam's own client renders here (CEF), as do the Rockstar and Ubisoft sign-in windows; their account services were the wall in testing, not the engine.

Why it exists: Wine 10 (the default engine) cannot start the EA app's vital background service or run its .NET setup steps, and its winemac lacks the cross-process remote-layer route that the Rockstar and Ubisoft launchers' browsers need (highball#15, #56, #60). This tree carries Highball's patches for both.

Three patches make the tree behave like the default engine: the Windows user follows the macOS user (CrossOver hack 12735 reverted), WINEDLLPATH_PREPEND is honoured so the renderer overlays apply, and wined3d's automatic renderer is OpenGL first as upstream. winemac.so exports macdrv_functions, so the DXMT and D3DMetal bridges work. This engine ships no winemetal.dll of its own; the DXMT overlay carries it. Wine Mono and Gecko are included.

DXMT here is Highball's branch (cross-process swapchains, DXMT_ALLOW_CROSS_PROCESS_SWAPCHAIN=1), needed by the EA client. D3DMetal is the Template's 3.0 with the timestamp shim in front, as on the default engine. Accepted licences carry over when a bottle moves.
Moving a bottle here re-runs the Windows setup (different Wine build); moving back is the same step. Nothing installed in the bottle is removed either way.
